Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety

which anxiety, and how to treatAre the attacks unexpected, and have a substance and a medical cause been excluded?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Exclude a cause first: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) glucose urine toxicology; consider an ECG (electrocardiogram) for palpitations or chest pain
  • Recurrent unexpected attacks 1 month or more of worry or behavior change panic disorder; no test makes it
  • CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or venlafaxine XR (extended release), or both; start the drug low, raise slowly; benzodiazepine short term only
What it is

Recurrent unexpected attacks worry about more of them or avoidance of their triggers

Attack: abrupt surge of fear peak within minutes 4 or more of 13 symptoms

Driver

Proposed: catastrophic reading of normal body sensations

Triggers

Affected first-degree relative non-modifiable female: about 2 times as often as men non-modifiable

Anxious temperament stressful life events

Chain

Proposed: body sensation appraised as catastrophic fear peaks within minutes

Worry about the next attack avoidance of attack triggers

Insights

Attacks occur in other anxiety disorders too ask what the fear is about

Lactate can provoke attacks more often than in healthy people no standardized criteria a known finding, not a diagnostic test

Who, mechanism and coursedetail behind the chain
WhoUsually starts in late adolescence or early adulthood; uncommon before age 14; women affected about twice as often as men
FamilyRaised risk in first-degree relatives
MechanismProposed: oversensitive carbon dioxide detectors in the medulla, causing hypocapniasodium lactate, carbon dioxide, caffeine and yohimbine can provoke attacks more than in healthy controls
CourseMost relapse even after a symptom-free period; only about 60% remit within 6 months
2Urgent risks
HeartPalpitations or chest pain
Regular, abrupt on and off: SVT (supraventricular tachycardia) may be misread as panic

If palpitations or chest pain occur, choose an ECG. Guideline detailPalpitations: preexcitation or a short or long QT interval; chest pain: ischemia, infarction or pericarditis

Blood pressureSevere hypertension during the episodes

If the blood pressure is severely high in a spell, choose plasma free metanephrines.

SubstanceStimulant or cannabis intoxication, or alcohol withdrawal, can precipitate attacks

If attacks occur only during intoxication or withdrawal from the substance, choose substance-induced attacks, not panic disorder.

SuicidePanic disorder can lead to depression; suicidal ideation and substance use are more likely

If panic disorder is diagnosed, choose asking about suicidal ideation, depression and substance use.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected attacks peaking within minutes1 month or more of worry about more attacks or a behavior change
AgoraphobiaAvoids crowds, lines, public transportation, open or enclosed places, or being out aloneEscape hard or help unavailable, in 2 or more of 5 situations; typically 6 months or more; with panic disorder, give both
Social anxiety disorderAttacks only in social situations with possible scrutinyFear of negative evaluation, not of the attacks; typically 6 months or more
Specific phobiaAttacks only with one feared triggerOne object or situation, almost always immediate fear; not 2 of 5; typically 6 months or more
Generalized anxiety disorderExcessive worry about a number of events, hard to controlAt least 6 months, more days than not; 3 or more of 6 symptoms (1 in children)
Preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness; mild or no symptomsAt least 6 months; persistent, while panic is typically acute and episodic
Distressing body symptoms with disproportionate thoughts, high health anxiety or excessive time spentTypically more than 6 months symptomatic; panic anxiety is typically acute and episodic
Weight loss, heat intolerance, resting tachycardia, tremorLow TSH, high free thyroxine
Stimulant or cannabis intoxication; withdrawal from a depressant such as alcohol or a barbiturateAttacks only during intoxication or withdrawal from the substance; history and urine toxicology
Episodic headache, sweating, racing heartSevere hypertension in the episodes; raised plasma free metanephrines
SVT (supraventricular tachycardia) or another arrhythmiaRegular fast palpitations; abrupt start, abrupt stopRegular, abrupt on and off; ECG ideally during an episode; Holter or event monitoring may be needed
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Weight loss, heat intolerance, resting tachycardiaHyperthyroidismTSH; a high free thyroxine confirms
Severe hypertension with headache and sweating in spellsPheochromocytomaPlasma free metanephrines
Palpitations that start and stop abruptly, regular and fastSVT or preexcitationECG before calling them panic attacks

Pause point. The bait: a lactate challenge offered to confirm panic disorder; no test confirms it, and lactate challenges lack standardized criteria. But when the question asks which abnormality the patient most likely has, increased sensitivity to lactate is the answer.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: panic disorder Attacks – recurrent unexpected panic attacks; each an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort, peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms (STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's) · Aftermath – at least 1 month, after at least 1 attack, of persistent worry about more attacks or their consequences, or a significant maladaptive behavior change, such as avoidance, tied to the attacks · Cause – not attributable to a substance or another medical condition · Other – not better explained by another mental disorder
STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's
  • S – sweating
  • T – trembling
  • U – unsteadiness, dizziness
  • D – depersonalization, derealization
  • E – excessive heart rate, palpitations
  • N – nausea
  • T – tingling
  • S – shortness of breath
  • FEAR – of dying, of losing control, of going crazy
  • C – chest pain, chills, choking
7Treatment
1

1st lineat diagnosis

CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or venlafaxine XR (extended release), or both
2

Bridgesevere symptoms or coexisting conditions before the antidepressant works

A benzodiazepine such as alprazolam, short term only

Added to an antidepressant, it may speed recovery but does not improve longer-term outcomes; tolerance and dependence are risks.

3

Second line, after first-line options faildrug ineffective after at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range

Clomipramine, imipramine or mirtazapine

Guideline detailPsychDB also lists benzodiazepines as second line

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Starting the SSRIFor most, half the usual depression starting dose; raise about every 7 daysEarly activation makes many patients stop it
Severe symptoms before the SSRI worksA benzodiazepine such as alprazolam as a bridgeShort term only; not as the only treatment
History of substance useAn SSRI with CBT; no benzodiazepine bridgeIf another drug is needed: gabapentin and mirtazapine are recommended; hydroxyzine may be an alternative
Palpitations invite a beta-blockerAn SSRI, not propranololPropranolol is not recommended for panic disorder
Buspirone offeredAn SSRI insteadHelps generalized anxiety; does not appear effective for panic disorder
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Little change after 2 weeks at a low doseRaise the dose; not ineffective until at least 4 weeks at the high end of the range
Some meaningful improvement at 4 to 6 weeksAllow several months before judging the full effect
Symptoms improvedContinue the drug for 12 months, then taper, to limit relapse; most have a recurrence even after a symptom-free period
Ongoing careWatch for depression, disability, alcohol and substance use, suicidal ideation; ask about agoraphobia, which commonly co-occurs
Practice
  1. 32-year-old woman, 8 months of episodes racing heart, sweating, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; some at rest 7 months avoiding buses, crowds, lines: no escape or help oriented, anxious about the next · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, toxicology normal → Panic disorder and agoraphobia → unexpected attacks plus fear of 2 or more situations where escape is hard; when criteria for both are met, both are assigned
  2. 41-year-old man, 9 months of worry, more days than not about job, finances, children's safety; cannot switch it off restless, tired, tense; sleeps poorly No sudden episodes of intense fear alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH normal → Generalized anxiety disorder → excessive worry about a number of events, hard to control, more days than not for at least 6 months, with at least 3 of 6 symptoms; the worry is not about attacks
  3. 23-year-old man, 10 months of pounding heart, sweating, shaking only when presenting in class or eating in the cafeteria fears others will see him blush, think him foolish now skips those classes alert, oriented, euthymic · afebrile; vitals, toxicology normal → Social anxiety disorder → the attacks come only in social situations, and the fear is of negative evaluation, not of the attacks
  4. 27-year-old woman, 1 year of intense fear, sweating, racing heart begins within seconds whenever she must ride an elevator climbs 12 flights of stairs to avoid it No episodes at other times alert, oriented, euthymic · vital signs normal → Specific phobia → one situation almost always provokes immediate fear and is avoided; one situation is not the 2 of 5 that agoraphobia needs
  5. 34-year-old woman, 5 months of unexpected spells: choking, nausea, chills, shaking each peaks within minutes and ends; no symptoms between spells dreads the next spell and fears a hidden disease; no drug use HR 74/min · TSH, glucose, ECG, toxicology normal → Panic disorder → unexpected spells that peak within minutes and clear completely, with worry about further attacks, are panic disorder; in somatic symptom disorder the physical symptoms persist over time, and generalized anxiety disorder needs excessive worry about multiple issues, not only about the attacks
  6. 36-year-old woman, 14 months of fear that she has heart disease checks her pulse many times a day has seen three cardiologists No sudden fear episodes; occasional mild chest tightness alert, oriented, anxious, not delusional · afebrile; vitals, ECG, echocardiogram normal → Illness anxiety disorder → persistent preoccupation with a serious illness for at least 6 months with mild or no symptoms; health anxiety in panic disorder is acute and episodic
  7. 29-year-old woman, 3 months of feeling anxious and shaky, with palpitations lost 5 kg (11 lb) without trying feels hot when others are comfortable alert, oriented, restless · HR 112/min · BP 138/70 mm Hg · warm, moist skin · fine hand tremor → Serum TSH → weight loss, heat intolerance and resting tachycardia point to hyperthyroidism; a low TSH screens, and a high free thyroxine confirms
  8. 38-year-old man, 4 months of spells pounding headache, drenching sweats, racing heart each lasts 15 to 30 minutes Alert, oriented, euthymic BP 196/112 mm Hg in a spell, 150/94 between · HR 104/min · TSH 2.1 μU/mL · glucose 96 mg/dL → Plasma free metanephrines → episodes of severe hypertension with headache, sweating and a racing heart point to pheochromocytoma
  9. 22-year-old man, 2 months of sudden episodes racing heart, lightheadedness and fear they start and stop abruptly Alert, oriented, euthymic HR 76/min and BP 122/78 mm Hg between episodes · TSH, glucose and urine toxicology normal → Electrocardiogram → palpitations call for an ECG to look for preexcitation before the episodes are called panic attacks
  10. 26-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; 3 months worrying about the next wants a diagnostic test oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, ECG, toxicology normal → Sertraline at a low starting dose and CBT → criteria are met and the mimics are excluded; no test makes the diagnosis, and a lactate challenge has no standardized criteria
  11. 34-year-old man, 6 months of recurrent unexpected episodes intense fear with sweating, palpitations, dizziness, trembling stopped driving 5 months ago, fearing another asks for something to stop them alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → Escitalopram, started low and titrated → an SSRI is first line; a benzodiazepine alone does not improve longer-term outcomes, and propranolol is not recommended
  12. 28-year-old woman, 5 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, chest pain, fear of losing control months of worry started sertraline 50 mg daily 5 days ago now jittery, more anxious; wants to stop oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 88/min → Lower the dose, then raise it slowly → initial activation can be troubling; start at half the usual depression dose and increase about every 7 days
  13. 31-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying months of worry sertraline 25 mg daily for 2 weeks: little change No adverse effects alert, oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 78/min · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Raise the sertraline dose → a drug is not ineffective until it has been given for at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range
  14. 25-year-old man, 2 months of unexpected fear episodes palpitations, choking, sweating, chest pain; many a day housebound 6 weeks; cannot work started sertraline yesterday No substance use history oriented · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → A benzodiazepine for the first weeks → with severe symptoms, a benzodiazepine such as alprazolam bridges until the antidepressant takes effect; short term only
  15. 40-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, abstinent 2 months 5 months of recurrent unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying avoids leaving home alone alert, oriented, euthymic · vitals, TSH, ECG normal · urine toxicology negative → Alprazolam → benzodiazepines are avoided with a history of substance use; gabapentin and mirtazapine are recommended
  16. 33-year-old woman treated with sertraline and CBT for recurrent unexpected episodes of fear no episodes for 3 months asks to stop the drug alert, euthymic · HR 70/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Continue it for 12 months, then taper → once symptoms improve, continue the drug for 12 months before tapering to limit relapse
How NBME framed it: question 1

25-year-old woman, 2 months of sudden anxiety episodes, several times a week chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations fears losing control and going crazy says they come out of the blue Not depressed; sleep and appetite unchanged 170 cm, 60 kg, BMI (body mass index) 21 kg/m² · pulse 88/min · BP 130/86 mm Hg · physical and mental status examinations normal · laboratory studies normal · urine toxicology negative

Which abnormality is she most likely to have?

Competing answers
  • Abnormal eye tracking: “going crazy” suggests psychosis; but abnormal eye tracking goes with schizophrenia, and her mental status examination is normal.
  • Delayed rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on polysomnography: the stem mentions sleep; but it goes with sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder and some drugs and alcohol, not panic disorder.
  • Enlarged third and lateral ventricles on head CT (computed tomography): a structural brain cause; but aqueductal stenosis, the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus, is atypical in a healthy young adult and does not explain the attacks.
  • Cortisol not suppressed by 1 mg of dexamethasone: a stress-axis test; but nonsuppression points to Cushing syndrome, not panic disorder.

Down to two: increased sensitivity to lactate infusions or cortisol nonsuppression. Lactate: recurrent attacks that come out of the blue, with a normal workup, point to panic disorder (NBME's key), and patients with it have attacks in response to lactate at an increased rate (the explanation ties this to catastrophic appraisal of body states). Its diagnostic utility is unclear: there are no standardized criteria. The stem never states worry or avoidance, and the lead-in asks for a finding, not the diagnosis.

Pairs with Hypertension in an Adult: is the blood pressure severely high during the episodes? Thyroid Disease in an Adult: constant symptoms with weight loss? SSRI (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor) Adverse Effects: did the restlessness start with the drug? Bipolar Disorder: episodes of elevated mood?
Transferable rule

Exclude a substance and a medical cause first. Then name what the fear is about: the attacks themselves, negative evaluation, one object or situation, difficult escape, a number of events, or a serious illness.
